title: Alginate Treatment Delays Post-Harvest Softening of Blueberries
metaDescription: A study analyzes how alginate oligosaccharides help preserve blueberry firmness and quality during storage at 20 °C.
excerpt: Researchers evaluated the effect of alginate oligosaccharides in reducing water loss, regulating antioxidant enzymes and slowing post-harvest softening in blueberries.
imageAlt: Fresh, firm blueberries arranged in a wooden container on a natural background.

blocks.text: Introduction: the post-harvest challenge for blueberries

Blueberries are fruits recognized for their pleasant flavor and nutritional profile. However, they face a considerable biological challenge once harvested: their shelf life is relatively short when stored at room temperatures close to 20 °C. Under such conditions, the fruit tends to soften and deteriorate quickly, which directly affects its texture and appearance.

Understanding the biochemical processes that trigger the loss of firmness is crucial for developing post-harvest technologies able to protect fruit quality without altering its natural properties. For this reason, the scientific community is investigating innovative treatments designed to slow cellular degradation and extend preservation time.
What the source says: treatment with alginate oligosaccharides

According to research published in the Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry, the use of alginate oligosaccharides (AOS) proved to be an effective alternative to delay the softening of blueberries stored at 20 °C after harvest.

The study revealed that AOS application reduced internal water loss in the fruit. At the same time, it increased the enzymatic activity and gene expression of key antioxidant defenses, among them superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase (CAT), peroxidase (POD) and ascorbate peroxidase (APX). This antioxidant activation reduced the accumulation of reactive species such as the superoxide anion (O2-) and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), as well as lowering levels of malondialdehyde (MDA), an indicator linked to metabolic stress in cells.

In parallel, the researchers observed that the treatment reduced the activity and gene expression of the enzymes in charge of degrading the cell wall, such as polygalacturonase (PG), carboxymethylcellulase (Cx), β-galactosidase (β-Gal) and β-glucosidase (β-Glu). This inhibition helped preserve cell wall integrity, maintain firmness and slow softening. Likewise, AOS treatment reduced weight loss and the rate of rot, keeping both the acidity and the soluble solids of the product stable.
Context: the cell wall and oxidative stress

Post-harvest softening of blueberries does not happen in isolation; it is the direct consequence of a series of physiological events where dehydration, oxidative attack on membranes and the gradual dismantling of the pectic structures of the cell wall converge.

At 20 °C, the fruit’s metabolism speeds up the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and the action of enzymes such as PG or Cx. The contribution of the research was to show that alginate oligosaccharides act in a coordinated way: they mitigate water loss, boost the internal antioxidant shield (SOD, CAT, POD, APX) and slow the enzymatic breakdown of the cell wall, extending the fruit’s commercial stability.
What it means for you: preservation and freshness in fruit

Although this work was carried out at the laboratory and post-harvest research level, its conclusions offer valuable information on the factors that affect blueberry durability. Understanding that dehydration and enzymatic activity speed up texture loss highlights the importance of careful handling from the moment of picking.

For consumers, firmness is one of the most appreciated attributes when biting into a fresh blueberry. Advances in post-harvest treatments such as alginate oligosaccharides hint at future applications that keep the balance between sugars (soluble solids), acidity and firm texture for longer during storage at room temperature.

In conclusion, alginate oligosaccharide treatment represents a useful post-harvest strategy to coordinate cell wall and reactive oxygen species metabolism at 20 °C, reducing rot, weight loss and softening of blueberries while preserving their soluble solids and acidity.
